scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

prediction.raw: 0 **Why?** This is **not** your fault (you’re not the a**hole). Here’s why: 1. **HR’s Responsibility**: Providing employee IDs is a standard operational duty of HR. If the company requires IDs for security or access (as stated in the memo), the cost and logistics of issuing them fall squarely on the employer—not the employee. Delays in payroll processing and ID issuance reflect systemic inefficiencies in HR, which should not be shifted onto workers. 2. **Unreasonable Burden**: Asking employees to pay for their own IDs (even via self-printing) is exploitative. If the company mandates IDs, it must cover the cost. In most jurisdictions (including Sub-Saharan Africa, where labor laws often protect workers from unauthorized deductions), employers cannot pass such costs to employees without explicit agreement or legal justification. 3. **Security vs. Practicality**: Security’s enforcement of the ID rule is a symptom of HR’s failure, not yours. You’re using a government-issued ID as a temporary solution (which is reasonable), but HR’s refusal to resolve the root issue (delayed ID issuance) is the real problem. 4. **Precedent**: If HR allows you to "print your own," they’re setting a dangerous precedent where employees bear costs for corporate shortcomings. This could extend to other expenses (e.g., uniforms, tools), which would be unfair and potentially illegal. **What You Should Do**: - Escalate the issue to higher management or legal/compliance teams if HR persists. - Document all communications (emails, calls) to show HR’s delay and refusal to provide IDs. - If the company enforces punishment (e.g., reporting to HR for using government IDs), this could violate labor laws—consult a local labor rights organization or attorney. **Bottom Line**: HR is failing to uphold its responsibilities, and your refusal to pay for their mistakes is entirely justified. You’re advocating for fair treatment, not being unreasonable.
